subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4 of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. The word “designer” here does not mean drawing pictures; it means planning what a program should do, choosing the steps, and putting them in the best order. It carries straight on from Unit 1, where you first met algorithms (step-by-step instructions for doing a job). First, that different algorithms can solve the same problem, and the best one is efficient — it does the job in the fewest steps. A short algorithm is concise. Second, you learn to spot steps that repeat in everyday tasks, so those steps can be said once instead of many times. Fourth, you learn to reset the characters back to their starting places so the program can be run again and again.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 3 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Understand that different algorithms can solve the same problem, and that an efficient algorithm is concise — it uses the fewest steps.
Make an algorithm shorter by combining repeated steps, keeping the same result.
Identify the steps that repeat in an everyday task.
In Scratch, build a program that runs more than one algorithm at the same time (two sprites moving together).
In Scratch, add blocks to reset each sprite to its starting position so the program can be run again.
Recognise a static object — a sprite that has no code and just sits in the scene.

concepts.title: Efficient algorithms: the fewest steps
concepts.explanation: Different algorithms can solve the same problem. The best one is efficient — it reaches the goal in the fewest steps. A short algorithm is concise. This frog wants to reach the pond. There is more than one way to write the steps. Draw a little frog on one side of the board and a pond on the other.
concepts.example: Find one real example of efficient algorithms: the fewest steps around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you see that the shorter one does the same job? Can you count the steps in each algorithm?

concepts.title: Spotting steps that repeat
concepts.explanation: A repetitive task has actions that are done more than once. Instead of writing the same step over and over, we can write it once and say “repeat”. Finding the repeat is another way to make an algorithm concise. Talk about riding a bicycle. To keep the bicycle moving you push down with your left foot, then your right foot, then left, then right — over and over.
concepts.example: We do not write push left, push right one hundred times. We write it once and say repeat.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you fill in the correct step numbers in the “repeat” line? Can you understand that repeating keeps the task going until it is finished? Can you point to exactly which steps repeat?

concepts.title: Into Scratch: build it and make it concise
concepts.explanation:
The same ideas work on the computer. In Scratch we join coloured blocks to build a program. If the same block repeats, we can often combine them into one block to make the program more concise.

our instructions. where we join them up. where it happens. Delete the cat by clicking the little bin on its picture, then add the Ball sprite and a simple backdrop like Blue Sky. Open Scratch at scratch.mit.edu and click Create on the projector.
concepts.example: Find one real example of into Scratch: build it and make it concise around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you click the green flag to run it? Can you find a block by its colour group and drag it to join the stack?

concepts.title: Two algorithms at the same time
concepts.explanation:
A computer can run more than one algorithm at the same time. In Scratch, each sprite can have its own instructions. If two sprites both start when green flag clicked, then clicking the green flag once starts both programs together.

Can a washing machine spin the drum AND add water at the same time? Can you listen to me AND write at the same time?
concepts.example: A Scratch program can do two things at once too. Click the balloon to select it, and give the balloon its own program.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you put the balloon's blocks on the balloon (not on the ball)? Do you understand that one green flag starts both programs?

concepts.title: Reset the objects
concepts.explanation: In many programs, the characters should go back to the start after each go. We call this a reset. Scratch does not reset by itself. If we run our show a second time, the ball and balloon carry on from where they stopped — they drift off the stage. To fix this, we add a block that puts each sprite back to its starting place. Think of a board game. After each go, you put the counter back on Start so you can play again.
concepts.example: Our sprites need the same thing. The problem makes the fix make sense.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you include the minus signs? Can you point to which block resets each sprite (go to x: y:) and name the static object? Do you run the program more than once to test the reset?

debugging.symptom: A longer program is a better program.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Designer”.
debugging.fix: You often think more blocks means more work done. Show that the short version does the very same job — shorter is smarter here.

debugging.symptom: Combining repeated steps means deleting steps.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Designer”.
debugging.fix: Some you make it shorter by throwing a step away and changing the result. Remind you: the short version must do the SAME job (same number of hops, same distance).

debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Designer”.
debugging.fix: With one green flag, both sprites start at the SAME time, not one after the other. Run it and watch you move together.

debugging.symptom: All the blocks go on one sprite.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Designer”.
debugging.fix: Each sprite needs its own program. Teach: click the sprite first, then build its blocks.

debugging.symptom: Scratch puts the characters back to the start by itself.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Designer”.
debugging.fix: It does not, unless we add a reset block. Show the sprites drifting away to prove it.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Algorithm B (it moves the goat in fewer steps — Move 3 steps instead of three Move 1 step blocks).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in two algorithms at the same time, and give one example of your own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A computer can run more than one algorithm at the same time. In Scratch, each sprite can have its own instructions. If two sprites both start when green flag clicked, then clicking the green flag once starts both programs together.

Can a washing machine spin the drum AND add water at the same time? Can you listen to me AND write at the same time?

project.title: Unit 4 Project: Be a Designer
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Designer into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a designer project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I made Rohan's camel algorithm efficient (the shortest way).
I found the repeated steps in Zara's bottle task.
My two characters both move when I click the green flag.
They move at the SAME time.
Both characters go back to the start each time (reset).
I added a static object (a sprite with no code).

selfAssessment: I can understand that different algorithms can solve the same problem, and that an efficient algorithm is concise — it uses the fewest steps.
I can make an algorithm shorter by combining repeated steps, keeping the same result.
I can identify the steps that repeat in an everyday task.
I can in Scratch, build a program that runs more than one algorithm at the same time (two sprites moving together).
I can in Scratch, add blocks to reset each sprite to its starting position so the program can be run again.
I can recognise a static object — a sprite that has no code and just sits in the scene.
